Removing rejection does not remove the rest of the setting. Anonymity, earned entitlement, experimenter observation, and whether the menu allows taking as well as giving can change the meaning of the action. The progression across @fig-social-preference-games-redraw shows which rights and options change between games. These contrasts narrow the explanation without turning a transfer into a pure measure of generosity.

Sharing notes may matter because the other person responds in kind. In two fMRI experiments involving 36 women, Rilling and colleagues (2002) found that mutual cooperation with a presumed human partner was associated with stronger responses in parts of the ventral striatum and orbitofrontal cortex than the average of the other three Prisoner's Dilemma outcomes. Mutual cooperation paid less than exploiting a cooperating partner. The pattern therefore cannot be read as a simple ranking of the immediate cash payoff.

The measurement was **blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) activity**, an indirect indicator of neural activity. It did not measure dopamine release. The findings support a role for reward processing in mutual cooperation; they do not establish that cooperation always releases more dopamine than defection. This is the same distinction between brain activity and neurotransmitter release discussed in [Chapter 21](21-habits-wanting-and-self-control.qmd#research-near-miss-evidence).

Social preferences can also make another person's loss attractive. Someone who has been deliberately betrayed may be willing to pay to punish the offender, even when doing so cannot recover the lost money. The prospect of seeing a wrong answered may itself enter the payoff.

De Quervain and colleagues (2004) studied this possibility using **positron emission tomography (PET)** during a trust game. After a partner kept money instead of returning a share, participants could assign punishment points. Effective punishment reduced the partner's earnings; symbolic punishment did not. While participants considered their response, effective punishment produced greater activity in the **dorsal striatum**, a region involved in reward processing and goal-directed action. Stronger activation was also associated with willingness to spend more of one's own money to punish.

The authors interpreted this pattern as evidence of **anticipated satisfaction from punishment**. A monetary sacrifice can therefore be consistent with pursuing something the person values. The term *altruistic punishment* does not establish a selfless psychological motive: enforcing a cooperative norm and expecting personal satisfaction can coexist.

How literally should we take the idea that “revenge is sweet”? Reward-related brain activity is not a direct measure of experienced pleasure, and the study did not establish that striatal activation caused punishment. Its analysis included 14 men who had trusted their partners, which also limits generalization. As [Chapter 6](06-valuation-how-options-become-worth-choosing.qmd#research-lens-value-is-distributed-not-a-single-center) explains, a brain region's involvement cannot uniquely identify a mental experience.

For the colleagues sharing notes, this creates a practical tension. Wanting an exploiter to face consequences can motivate enforcement, but the appeal of retaliation does not establish that it will repair the relationship. A useful sanction needs to be judged by what happens to cooperation as well as by how satisfying it seems to impose.

Changing a rule may also change its social meaning. Gneezy and Rustichini's (2000) daycare study found that introducing a fine for late pickup increased lateness in the treated centers; the effect did not simply disappear when the fine was removed. One interpretation is that parents began to treat lateness as a service they could buy instead of an imposition they should avoid. The result makes the relationship between incentives and obligation part of the design problem. The applied notes examine this study alongside fairness in markets and punishment.

Favoritism does not necessarily mean hostility. In a meta-analysis of 212 studies, Balliet and colleagues (2014) found greater cooperation with ingroup than outgroup members. Comparisons with unclassified strangers supported a pattern driven mainly by extra cooperation toward insiders, rather than reduced cooperation toward outsiders. The practical distinction matters: someone can sincerely deny disliking another department while giving their own colleagues preferential help. The size of that difference depends on the task, information, and relationship.

These are complementary levels of explanation: experiments examine responses to group labels, whereas the model tracks the spread of conditional strategies. The model does not establish that human favoritism is inevitable. It also keeps the rule for identifying insiders fixed. Shared goals matter because people can change which boundary defines the group whose success they value.

Sherif's (1958) account of the Robbers Cave camp study gives a concrete illustration. Researchers first established two groups of boys, then introduced competitive activities and prizes that generated hostility. Pleasant contact alone did not dissolve the rivalry. Later, the researchers arranged problems requiring joint effort, including restoring a water supply and getting transport working to collect food. Across a series of shared tasks, hostility declined and friendships increasingly crossed the group boundary.

The sequence matters: repeated cooperation supplied experiences of being useful to one another. This was a staged field study with a deliberately homogeneous sample, not a clean comparison isolating one task or a universal cure for conflict. It changed both interdependence and social experience; it does not establish that a change in identity alone produced the improvement.

Gaertner and colleagues (1990) tested this account with pairs of three-person groups, varying cooperation and whether participants were encouraged to see one group or two. Among participants initially encouraged to see two groups, cooperation strengthened the perception of a single group and reduced evaluative bias. The findings support recategorization as a pathway; they do not establish that it is the only mechanism or that warmer evaluations guarantee lasting cooperation.

Levine and colleagues (2005) illustrate how the boundary can also shape helping. In one study, football supporters whose club identity had been emphasized were more likely to help an apparently injured stranger wearing their own team's shirt than a rival team's or an unbranded shirt. In a second study, emphasizing the broader identity of football supporter extended helping to rival fans, but not equally to people without a football shirt. The two-study pattern suggests that a more inclusive identity can widen concern while leaving a boundary in place; it does not show durable reconciliation between rival groups.

An inclusive identity need not require either department to abandon its expertise or history. A **dual identity** preserves subgroup membership within a wider “we”: two distinct departments contributing to one service. Dovidio and colleagues (2009) also warn that an emphasis on sameness can obscure unequal treatment. A common identity is more credible when people can name differences and challenge unfair arrangements without being accused of undermining unity.

These are design implications, not a guaranteed intervention package. Check whether help actually crosses the old boundary and persists after the initial task. Better relations can make cooperation easier, but they cannot make an exploitative agreement fair or remove a remaining incentive to free-ride.

Return to the joint report. Individual assessment may reward withholding useful notes; colleagues may doubt that anyone will reciprocate; they may disagree about what can legitimately be shared; or they may reserve help for their own department. Recognizing shared work addresses the first problem, a small reciprocal trial with visible contributions can address the second, and an agreed disclosure rule can address the third. A joint task with complementary roles can help bridge a group boundary. The response should follow the reason for withholding rather than treating every refusal as the same problem.

For an application to group boundaries, choose two teams that cooperate internally but struggle to help one another. Propose a superordinate goal and specify each team's contribution. Separate the incentive change from the identity change you expect: what would people gain, and whom might they begin to count as “us”? Identify observable help across teams and a follow-up check after the task, rather than treating agreement with a team slogan as evidence of restored cooperation.

Evolutionary game theory studies how success in an interaction affects the persistence or spread of strategies. A strategy here need not be a consciously chosen plan: it can be an inherited behavioral rule. **Evolutionary stability** asks whether a resident strategy can resist a sufficiently rare alternative under the model's conditions; it is distinct from an individual's calculation about an opponent (Maynard Smith & Price, 1973).

A spatial model adds rules for interaction or movement. Cooperators may persist in clusters where much of the benefit they provide reaches other cooperators. Whether that happens depends on the network, payoffs, and update rule; simply drawing a network does not establish a cooperation advantage.

Tournament success, repeated-game equilibrium, and evolutionary stability are different criteria. Tit-for-tat's tournament performance does not make it successful under every population process (Axelrod, 1984; Imhof et al., 2007). A dynamic model needs declared payoffs, initial conditions, transmission or update rules, interaction structure, and time horizon; a stochastic simulation also needs recorded random seeds and independent runs. [Appendix B](../appendices/appendix-b-evolutionary-explanations-of-value-choice-and-rationality.qmd#population-model-provenance) develops these requirements and separates evolutionary function, current mechanism, and normative interpretation.

Local reproduction creates clusters whose members tend to share markers and strategies. Mutual help can sustain these clusters, while selective helpers avoid the cost of helping differently marked neighbors. The marker does not guarantee cooperation: same-marker free riders can exploit a cooperative cluster. In Hammond and Axelrod's (2006) reported dynamics, selectively cooperative clusters of another marker can spread at those free riders' expense. Ingroup favoritism can therefore coexist with considerable cooperation while leaving a boundary across which help is withheld.

The connection to common goals has a limit. The model defines an insider by marker equality; it does not model rival departments learning to regard themselves as one team. The [shared-goal discussion](#superordinate-goals-and-cooperation) concerns changing that social boundary, not simply making a fixed ethnocentric rule more successful. A simulation of selective helping neither establishes the evolutionary history of human prejudice nor justifies exclusion.

If rejection changes across conditions, a model based only on final payoffs is incomplete. The contrast does not by itself prove negative reciprocity: perceived intent, responsibility, norm violation, or demand may have changed. The additional records reveal which explanation is plausible and which further treatment is needed.

These comparisons do not isolate culture from recruitment, comprehension, stakes, markets, kinship, or production systems. Meta-analysis likewise finds variation across settings (Oosterbeek et al., 2004). Use it to generate a specific hypothesis about entitlements or expectations, then test a contrast that separates that hypothesis from the other differences.

In a well-known capuchin comparison, a monkey that receives cucumber while a neighbor receives a preferred grape sometimes refuses the cucumber. Inequality aversion, frustration, changed reward expectation, and protest against the experimenter remain competing accounts; the demonstration does not establish a human moral concept of fairness (Brosnan & de Waal, 2003). Neural studies of inequality and equity–efficiency trade-offs likewise identify correlates consistent with social valuation, not a unique motive or stable moral type (Hsu et al., 2008; Tricomi et al., 2010). Comparative and neural evidence should determine the next discriminating contrast, not close the diagnosis.

Two further scenarios show how judgments depend on the transaction: 74% rated auctioning one scarce doll to the highest bidder unfair ($N=101$), and 91% rated a rent increase exploiting a tenant's location-specific dependence unfair ($N=157$). “Unfair” combines the two unfavorable response categories; these results come from separate samples rather than one pooled survey.

[^ch25-golden-balls]: Contestants selected into the program and experienced the prize inside a larger show. Split–Steal differs from a standard Prisoner’s Dilemma: Steal weakly, rather than strictly, dominates Split.

A hiring committee hears the chair describe a candidate as “an obvious leader.” Around the table, heads nod. One member had doubts about the work sample but now wonders whether the others saw something she missed; another shares those doubts but does not want to hold up the decision. Their agreement looks the same from outside, although one may be revising a belief and the other withholding it.

People often learn selectively from prestigious, successful, similar, or numerous others. Those cues can be useful when they track relevant knowledge (Henrich & Gil-White, 2001; Boyd & Richerson, 1985). They are also fallible: prestige can spill across domains, success can reflect luck, and a majority can repeat one person's claim. Shared attention and teaching make cultural learning possible, but they do not make each public signal accurate (Tomasello, 1999; Tomasello et al., 2005; Boyd et al., 2011).

First, observers need **relevant contact with the problem**. A thousand ratings from people who never used the difficult feature may be weaker than ten reports from users who completed the same task under similar constraints. Prestige can help locate expertise, but status earned in one domain does not automatically transfer to another.

Second, judgments need some **independence of evidence**. Independence does not mean that people never communicate. It means that their initial observations or reasons are not all copies of one visible claim. Ten analysts who used the same vendor report do not supply ten sources. Five interviewers who discussed a candidate after the first interview may have produced one shared impression rather than five assessments.

Fourth, the process needs an **aggregation and correction rule**. A mean forecast can pool independent numerical judgments; a structured discussion can surface reasons; a market price can reward information; a checklist can preserve a minority warning. Each rule loses something. Means can hide multimodality, discussion can amplify status, prices combine information with constraints, and checklists cannot anticipate every failure. The rule should fit what is being aggregated.

Asch’s line-judgment studies made the answer much easier to see. A participant compared a target line with three alternatives, but heard other people give their answers first. Those people were working with the experimenter and deliberately agreed on a wrong line in twelve critical trials. Across 123 male college students, **36.8% of critical responses** followed the wrong majority; a separate group of 37 judging independently made errors on **0.7%** of those comparisons (Asch, 1956). The first percentage describes responses across trials, not the proportion of people who always conformed.

Conformity is not inherently defective. Shared conventions make traffic, queues, meetings, and safety routines possible. The danger is that public agreement does not reveal private belief. Group size, task ambiguity, status, public response, and unanimity change the pressure; even one dissenter can make disagreement socially possible. The organizational question is therefore: **What would someone hesitate to say here, even if it were true?**

A **dynamic norm** reports a verified direction of change when the desired behavior is not yet common—for example, that more households are reducing food waste—rather than pretending that the majority has already changed (Sparkman & Walton, 2017). It describes a trend, not current majority status. [Choice Architecture](40-choice-architecture-the-environment-gets-a-vote.qmd#choice-architecture-the-environment-gets-a-vote) develops when this design can help and the safeguards it requires. People may also underdetect how strongly descriptive norms affect their own behavior, which is one reason introspection alone is a poor norm audit (Nolan et al., 2008).

The parallel routes in @fig-social-pathways show why convergence alone cannot identify either a cascade or conformity pressure. An informational cascade can arise because earlier actions appear informative even when dissent is safe. Normative conformity can arise because disagreement is socially costly even when nobody thinks the majority knows more. The routes can interact, but the evidence needed to test them differs.

Popularity may reflect quality and partly produce the success later used to validate it. The experimental comparison in @fig-cultural-market-study-redraw helps separate those directions by comparing conditions with and without visible download counts, something an ordinary bestseller list cannot do.

That dependence becomes especially useful when a practice contains knowledge the learner cannot yet inspect. It also creates the risk examined in the main chapter: copying can preserve a useful routine or reproduce an untested error.

The two outcomes in @fig-social-learning-culture show why observation and imitation do not automatically produce useful accumulation. Accumulation also requires some source of variation or innovation, sufficient transmission and retention, and processes that preserve, select, or correct practices across learners or generations. The mixture differs across settings.

At first glance, the chimpanzee looks more rational. It extracts the causal structure and ignores theater. Yet children's tendency toward overimitation may serve a different problem. A learner cannot always know which step is irrelevant. A tap, gesture, sequence, or preparation may carry hidden causal information, social meaning, safety value, or conventional significance. High-fidelity copying can preserve opaque practices until their function becomes clear (Lyons et al., 2007).

Adjusting to another person’s tempo can communicate attention. Using imitation to bypass their judgment turns apparent rapport into covert pressure; smoother interaction alone does not make that objective defensible.

Financial markets put behavioral explanations through a demanding test: stakes are high, professionals participate, and mistakes create opportunities for others. Yet a biased investor does not imply a biased market, because other traders may offset the error.
2. **No free lunch.** A public rule does not reliably earn abnormal return after appropriate risk and realistic costs.

The first two claims in @fig-finance-euro-efficiency do not automatically establish the third. A price can be difficult to beat and still differ from a later estimate of fundamental value. Conversely, a price can be noisy without offering a low-risk implementable profit.

To label a return abnormal, we must first say what return was expected. Suppose an asset earns 12%. That is not evidence of mispricing until we specify its risk, exposures, time period, benchmark, and costs.

A documented return pattern challenges a specified benchmark; it does not say whether the source is behavioral error, omitted risk, friction, model misspecification, or data mining. Finance offers thousands of securities, variables, transformations, and subperiods, so out-of-sample, after-cost, and post-publication evidence matters (Harvey et al., 2016). McLean and Pontiff (2016) found that average predictability declined after publication, consistent with both correction through trading and bias in initial discovery. A good company, a low price, and a high future return remain three different judgments.

Professional incentives can shorten the horizon precisely when a long-horizon correction is expected. An arbitrageur can be right eventually and insolvent first. Behavioral market outcomes therefore require both a source of biased demand and a reason better-informed capital does not fully offset it.

After Palm's first trading day, observed prices implied that the residual 3Com businesses were worth about negative $22 billion in Lamont and Thaler's (2003) calculation. Simple addition makes that hard to defend. Yet Palm shares were scarce to borrow, shorting was costly and risky, and the distribution was delayed and conditional. The case is unusually strong evidence of relative-value mispricing—and equally strong evidence that a visible inconsistency need not create a riskless free lunch.
The separate paths in @fig-asset-bubble-feedback allow a boom to begin with genuine innovation and later acquire a feedback component. Credit can amplify buying, but the loop does not require it.

This is often called the **greater fool theory**. The label is provocative, but the mechanism is precise: an anticipated resale price makes buying attractive even when the expected payouts from holding the asset do not. Disagreement and constraints on short selling can give this resale option value (Scheinkman & Xiong, 2003). When expectations reverse, many holders may want to exit together. Buyers need not disappear at every conceivable price; the danger is that sufficient buyers are unavailable near the prices sellers expected, so even a modest sale can require a large price concession.

A temporary recovery during the decline can encourage the belief that the market is returning to normal. But the labels in a cycle diagram are usually assigned with hindsight. They do not identify today's phase reliably, establish that early buyers were informed, or imply that every boom follows the same path. Stories such as the shoeshine boy whose stock tips supposedly prompted Joseph Kennedy to exit before 1929 express concern about widespread participation; they are anecdotes, not verified trading signals.

The familiar version depicts an entire nation gambling away its wealth. Goldgar's (2007) archival research instead finds a much more limited network of participants and much less evidence of economy-wide ruin. Exceptional quoted prices should not be treated as typical completed cash transactions. The episode illustrates speculative resale, the social formation of value, and the importance of trust in promises. It also illustrates a second hazard: a memorable story about irrationality can survive long after historians have challenged its details.

The South Sea Company combined a role in managing British government debt with expectations of overseas trade. Its privileges included participation in the trade in enslaved Africans. The scheme's appeal cannot be understood simply as investment in a productive business: debt conversion, political support, and expectations about future share demand also mattered. In 1720 its share price rose dramatically before collapsing (Kindleberger & Aliber, 2011; Odlyzko, 2020).

Isaac Newton's investment history makes the timing problem vivid. An experienced investor, he sold South Sea holdings during the rise and made a substantial profit, then bought back at much higher prices and suffered large losses. Odlyzko's (2020) reconstruction supports that sequence but also shows why a single exact loss figure is misleading: losses relative to initial wealth differ from losses relative to the wealth Newton could have retained after his early gains. The often-repeated £20,000 is an estimate, and he did not end bankrupt.

The behavioral lesson is the vulnerability of a successful exit to later regret. Watching a price continue to rise can turn a realized gain into a perceived missed opportunity. Newton's trades illustrate that problem, although the surviving records cannot establish his precise thoughts at each purchase.

The U.S. boom of the late 1920s accompanied real economic growth and enthusiasm for technologies and companies. Excitement extended across telephone, electrical-manufacturing, and radio companies. However, selecting spectacular winners cannot establish how the entire market performed. Buying shares on margin added a separate vulnerability: investors financed part of their purchases with borrowed money and could face demands for additional funds when prices fell. The October 1929 crash damaged wealth and confidence, but the subsequent Depression also involved banking panics, monetary contraction, and other failures. Treating the crash as its complete explanation misses those transmission mechanisms (Richardson et al., 2013).

The broader NASDAQ is not the same portfolio as a selected internet-stock index. Ofek and Richardson (2003) report that their equal-weighted internet index gained more than 1,000% from early 1998 through February 2000, then lost those gains by the end of 2000. Their evidence connects optimistic beliefs and short-sale restrictions to high prices, and the release of previously restricted shares to subsequent declines. The success of the internet as a technology did not guarantee that buyers would earn satisfactory returns at the prices they paid.

Beliefs about value and beliefs about the next price also diverged. Shiller (2013) reports that in spring 2000 only about 33% of institutional respondents and 28% of individual respondents in the Yale surveys regarded the market as not overvalued, although most expected it to rise over the following year. These are survey responses, not proof of each respondent's subsequent trades. They nevertheless show how widespread valuation doubts can coexist with expectations of further gains. Resale expectations and uncertainty about timing can sustain participation even when confidence in fundamental value is weak.

The U.S. housing boom connected a familiar asset to a complicated financing system. Buyers could justify higher prices through rents, housing services, limited supply, or lower financing costs, but expectations of continued appreciation also made purchasing and refinancing appear safer. A comparison with longer historical patterns asks whether rents, incomes, construction costs, and financing conditions plausibly supported the increase. Population growth alone cannot settle it, and national indexes conceal substantial regional differences.

The damage spread beyond housing. The S&P 500 lost about 57% between its October 2007 peak and March 2009 trough (Rich, 2013). Equity markets across many countries also fell during 2008. Comparing those declines requires specifying dates, price versus total returns, and currency. A foreign investor's dollar return can differ sharply from the same market's local-currency return. The explanatory task is to trace exposures and financing, rather than assume that simultaneous losses establish identical national bubbles.

On October 19, 1987, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 22.6% in one day. Proposed explanations include changing economic expectations, portfolio-insurance selling, and strains in market liquidity and trading systems (Bernhardt & Eckblad, 2013). A later rebound cannot establish that the preceding valuation was correct, just as a crash alone cannot prove that it was a bubble. The price path leaves the underlying mechanism to be investigated.

In a common baseline parameterization, the asset lasts 15 periods and each period's dividend is equally likely to be 0, 8, 28, or 60 cents. Averaging the four equally likely dividends gives 24 cents per period. Immediately before trading in the first period, 15 dividends remain, so the risk-neutral benchmark is 360 cents. It falls by 24 cents after each dividend opportunity, reaches 24 cents before the final dividend, and is zero after the asset expires. For comparison, an asset that pays 12 or 20 cents with equal probability has an expected dividend of 16 cents and an initial 15-period benchmark of $2.40. The two parameterizations should not be mixed.

Participants begin with cash and shares. In a **double auction**, buyers can submit bids and sellers can submit asks while observing other offers. Under the classroom implementation used here, an incoming order that crosses the best standing offer executes at that standing offer's price. A trader can buy to collect remaining dividends or to sell again during the experiment. A resale changes who receives those dividends; it does not add dividends to the asset.

Prices in many inexperienced markets begin below the expected-dividend benchmark, rise above it, and fall late in the session. Initial underpricing could reflect risk aversion or uncertainty about the task and other traders. Later overpricing cannot be explained merely by learning that the asset has a larger expected dividend: the distribution is already given. Still, an expected-value benchmark is not every risk-averse trader's certainty equivalent, and a price deviation alone does not identify the belief or preference producing it.

Bubble-like paths are not confined to groups of a dozen participants. Williams (2008) reports large computerized classroom markets, including one with 304 traders that exhibited a substantial boom and crash. Adding traders therefore does not automatically create independent judgments or eliminate feedback. These markets differ from professional exchanges in incentives and institutions, so their size establishes a useful possibility rather than complete field realism.

Many real assets do not mechanically lose one dividend's expected value each short trading period. A useful experimental design therefore pays interest on cash, provides an expected dividend each period, and adds a final redemption payment. Choosing the redemption payment appropriately offsets the shortening dividend horizon, so the risk-neutral discounted benchmark stays constant.

Bostian and Holt (2009) describe this design and report prices rising above the flat benchmark. Their higher-payment example illustrates how faster wealth accumulation can support larger price deviations. Because the dividend and interest processes change together, that comparison should not be described as a pure manipulation of initial cash. Experiments that vary initial cash directly provide complementary evidence (Caginalp et al., 1998).

@tbl-bubble-experimental-conditions distinguishes the interventions rather than treating all reductions in bubbles as evidence for one mechanism. In particular, supplying cash, allowing borrowing, delaying payouts, and permitting short sales alter different parts of the market.

The no-resale result is particularly demanding for a pure greater-fool explanation. If traders cannot profit by passing the asset on, some other source of demand must account for the deviation. Confusion, valuation errors, preferences, and features of the trading task remain candidates. Tucker and Xu (2024) reproduced bubbles in a related no-speculation design but highlighted consequences of the restrictions themselves, including asymmetric endowments and changing cash-to-asset ratios and scarcity as trading proceeds. Removing resale therefore does not isolate one alternative psychological mechanism. Likewise, less trading when another activity is available does not mean that every field bubble results from boredom.

A rising market does not imply that participants accurately predict its next movement. Holt et al. (2017) elicited short-term price forecasts and found that predictions typically trailed prices during the rise and remained above them during the decline. Forecast paths were too flat and did not generally anticipate the turning point. Haruvy et al. (2007) likewise show why measuring expectations adds information beyond observing transactions: the same purchase can reflect different views about value and future resale prices.

Equal expected payouts do not imply that every preference model assigns equal value. Attraction to positively skewed payoffs and overweighting a small chance of a large gain are possible interpretations, not separately identified mechanisms established by the price difference. The example connects asset trading to the treatment of small probabilities in [Prospect Theory](17-prospect-theory-gains-and-losses-begin-at-a-reference-point.qmd).

Individual differences also matter without translating automatically into market accuracy. Corgnet et al. (2015) found that higher cognitive reflection test scores were associated with higher earnings and trading more consistent with fundamentals. Bubbles occurred even when participants had earned their initial endowments through a task, although trading volume and earnings dispersion were higher with house money. A correlation between reflection and earnings does not establish that training on the test would prevent bubbles or that reflective traders can always overcome other participants' demand.

The suggestion that “Lehman Sisters” would have avoided the crisis is a memorable prompt for a hypothesis. The experiments supply a more conditional answer. Eckel and Füllbrunn (2015) found larger bubbles in all-male than all-female markets in their declining-value design. Their later study did not find a significant difference when gender composition was obscured (Eckel & Füllbrunn, 2017). Holt et al. (2017) found similar bubbles across gender groups with flat fundamentals and unobtrusive sorting, but larger bubbles among men in a declining-value robustness treatment.

Wang et al. (2018) further found that all-female groups in China produced bubbles comparable to those in all-male groups, and larger than those in all-female U.S. groups. This limits any claim that a single stable gender difference determines market outcomes. Cross-country comparisons also change more than one contextual feature and cannot isolate “culture” as if it were a randomly assigned treatment.

Nadler et al. (2018) tested a different question by experimentally administering testosterone or placebo to male participants. Testosterone administration generated larger and longer-lasting bubbles in that setting. This supports a causal claim about the administered intervention in that sample; it does not identify the source of male–female differences, describe all men's behavior, or show that naturally occurring hormone variation caused a historical crisis.

These experiments establish that known dividend distributions, an announced horizon, larger groups, or prior experience do not invariably prevent mispricing. They also let researchers test how liquidity, financing, information, and trading rules alter the outcome. Transporting the findings requires comparing those conditions with the field market of interest.[^ch27-laboratory-markets] A historical price chart establishes a trajectory; a controlled treatment comparison can establish the effect of a particular intervention. Neither alone supplies a universal explanation for bubbles.

Write both the fundamental story that would justify the price and the feedback story that would make it fragile. For each, name a discriminating observation. Even a high bubble probability does not reveal timing. Robust responses—limiting leverage and position size, stress-testing funding, preserving liquidity, and precommitting review conditions—may dominate a confident directional bet.

Policy should therefore target the mechanism rather than the label: disclosure targets information problems; underwriting standards, capital buffers, and leverage limits target fragility and loss propagation; consumer protection targets burden and informed choice. Each intervention carries false-positive costs from constraining a sustainable market and false-negative costs from leaving a dangerous mechanism unaddressed. Ask who receives the upside, who can exit, who carries the downside, and whether losses are absorbable or propagated through obligations to others.

Preserve the pre-purchase record to apply the [process–outcome distinction](01-how-decisions-should-be-made-and-how-they-actually-are.qmd#outcome-is-not-process). A later gain should test the recorded thesis rather than erase weaknesses in the reasoning that produced it.

The earnings announcement now poses a sharper question: what would have to be missing from the current price for buying at your available execution price to make sense? If the evidence does not answer it, a favorable headline alone cannot complete the argument. Keep the original record; later returns can then test a prediction instead of supplying a convenient explanation.

For an audit, record the published answer to each step and mark missing information rather than inventing a price, return, or model. A full reproduction additionally requires the original sample-construction rules, data vintage, corporate-action handling, code, and trading assumptions.

Read each row of @tbl-finance-anomalies from the historical finding through the behavioral possibility to the rival account: a familiar label alone cannot identify the mechanism or establish an implementable trade.

The manager may know more than the engineer: perhaps the component was tested yesterday, or the apparent fault is normal under these conditions. Deferring to relevant expertise can save time and coordinate action. Yet a managerial title alone does not establish that this evidence exists. If the engineer stops asking because disagreement seems disloyal, authority has changed the decision through the social cost of speaking.

Burger (2009) tested a modified version of a different Milgram condition, stopping after the learner’s protest at 150 volts. In his baseline group, 28 of 40 participants began the next task item and had to be stopped by the experimenter. This was willingness to continue at that point; the study did not observe whether they would reach 450 volts. Its earlier cutoff and screening procedures also underline why the original distressing protocol cannot simply be repeated under present ethical standards.

These studies do not tell us how often an engineer will defer to a manager. They make the conditions of deference worth examining. Lena may reasonably leave a wider safety assessment to management, provided the concern reaches someone who can assess it and accepts responsibility for responding. Before closing the issue, ask what evidence supports the reassurance and who checked it. A credential or title can help locate expertise; it cannot replace that connection between reasons and accountable action.

Suppose one of Lena’s colleagues privately shares her concern but says nothing after Sam’s reassurance. If everyone reads that silence as agreement, the group gains apparent confidence without gaining evidence. A cohesive team can coordinate quickly, yet protecting that agreement can make an objection feel like a personal betrayal. Janis (1982) made **groupthink** a familiar account of how pressure for concurrence could narrow the appraisal of evidence and alternatives in policy groups. In his model, antecedent conditions could produce self-censorship, pressure on dissenters, and an illusion of unanimity, followed by defective decision processes. The framework remains a useful warning that agreement can be socially produced rather than evidentially earned.

It is also contested. Aldag and Fuller (1993) found that research did not convincingly validate the complete syndrome or a simple path from its proposed characteristics to poor outcomes. Esser's (1998) review found mixed results and continuing heuristic value, while emphasizing theoretical and methodological problems. The responsible use of the term is therefore as an umbrella that prompts diagnosis, not as a diagnosis supplied by hindsight.

**A bad outcome, apparent unanimity, or cohesion alone does not establish groupthink.** A bad result can follow from uncertainty, missing expertise, poor incentives, implementation failure, or chance. Unanimity can reflect genuinely convergent evidence or shared values. A meta-analysis found no significant overall effect of cohesion on decision quality; poorer decisions appeared under additional conditions such as directive leadership, and the result depended partly on what “cohesion” meant (Mullen et al., 1994).

A safeguard earns its place by revealing evidence, disagreement, or responsibility that the group previously lacked. Psychological safety—a shared belief that interpersonal risk taking is safe—was associated with learning behavior in 51 work teams (Edmondson, 1999). That association gives a reason to examine the cost of speaking; it does not show that announcing an “open door” makes a workplace safe. A colleague who raises a concern needs to see it considered, with a response that makes the next concern possible to raise.

Stasser and Titus (1985) studied this problem by distributing information about candidates among group members. Some facts were shared; others were known to only one member. In the hidden-profile condition, combining the unshared facts could reveal an alternative that each person’s initial information made less attractive. Discussion tended to favor shared and preference-consistent information, so having the relevant facts somewhere in the group did not ensure that they shaped its choice.

An organization can make a similar comparison between private views and beliefs about colleagues’ views. Anonymous input may uncover concerns that a public “Any objections?” misses, although silence can also reflect fatigue, uncertainty, or lack of relevant information. The purpose is to discover what people think before deciding why they did not speak.

An invitation to speak may uncover a withheld doubt, but it still leaves Lena’s inspection unassigned. Naming an inspector solves that ownership problem without supplying evidence the inspector does not hold. An anonymous poll can expose mistaken beliefs about colleagues’ views, but it cannot create expertise absent from the group. A mismatched safeguard can leave everyone feeling that the matter has been handled while the original gap remains.

Expertise can guide judgment, but an instruction does not transfer moral accountability away from the actor or the institution that designed the role. [Persuasion](30-persuasion-changing-minds-means-updating-models.qmd#influence-cues-are-signals-not-buttons) extends this question to other signals that can inform a choice or exploit trust.

The safety email can now end differently: “Lena will inspect the component by 3 p.m. and post the evidence here. Until then, we will follow the existing safety procedure; if the inspection cannot be completed, Sam will escalate it.” Colleagues can still challenge the assessment, but they no longer need to guess who owns the next step.

Culture is often introduced through visible differences: language, food, clothing, ritual, or holiday. These matter, but they do not capture its decision function. Culture is a system through which people learn what events signify, which motives are legitimate, what emotions fit a situation, who may speak, what counts as fairness, and what kind of person an action reveals.

Culture does not eliminate agency. People inherit, combine, contest, and revise cultural repertoires. They may follow one script at home, another in a profession, and a third among friends. Knowing a local convention gives us a starting interpretation, which the person’s response may confirm or overturn.

A trait dimension is not a fixed personality type, a moral ranking, or an explanation of every action. Culture concerns shared meanings and practices; identity concerns who someone understands themselves to be; a trait concerns a pattern across observations. They can interact without becoming interchangeable. Before calling a quiet colleague introverted, establish whether the pattern persists across settings or reflects this meeting's hierarchy, language demands, or reception of disagreement. A country label cannot substitute for an individual's trait measurement, and one awkward meeting cannot supply it either.

Use cultural knowledge as a **hypothesis generator**: “Silence may protect face; how are concerns normally raised here?” This question leaves room for an answer. “People from that country do not disagree” ends the inquiry before the person can speak.

The related terms **individualism** and **collectivism** concern cultural emphases on personal autonomy and individual goals, or on group obligations and shared goals (Hofstede, 1980). A cultural pattern and a person's self-construal are different levels of description. A country average does not tell us which commitment this person will prioritize in this decision.

Akerlof and Kranton (2000) incorporated identity into economic analysis by showing that acting consistently with an identity can itself carry utility. Oyserman's (2009) identity-based motivation account adds that identity changes how difficulty is interpreted. Difficulty can mean “this is important work people like us persist in” or “this shows that people like me do not belong.”

A difficult task can communicate **challenge and investment**—“this matters, and support is available”—or **exclusion and incompetence**—“people like me do not belong here.” Identity-safe teaching keeps the intellectual standard clear while making belonging, support, representation, and paths to improvement credible. Brief belonging interventions illustrate how interpretations of adversity can affect persistence (Walton & Cohen, 2011). Credible support also requires adequate instruction, fair evaluation, resources, and structural access.

If the senior person speaks first, others do not reveal independent evidence under the same conditions. If dissent carries career risk, silence is not a clean measure of agreement. Hierarchy can therefore degrade the information available to the hierarchy itself.

**Honor** centers reputation for strength, loyalty, and willingness to answer threat or insult. Such a logic can become especially important where formal protection is unreliable and reputation deters exploitation. **Dignity** emphasizes worth that does not depend entirely on public reputation. Leung and Cohen (2011) show that face, honor, and dignity are cultural logics with substantial variation within as well as between societies.

The [team-learning problem from Chapter 28](28-authority-groupthink-and-shared-responsibility.qmd#match-the-safeguard-to-the-missing-step) has a cultural dimension: what happens here after someone admits an error or questions a senior colleague? Psychological safety depends on those recurring consequences, alongside the standards for preparation and performance (Edmondson, 1999). A values poster cannot answer that question; the next response to bad news can.

Begin by separating what you observed from what you inferred, then ask a local question: “I noticed the room became quiet; how are concerns usually raised?” Include people with less power, whose public behavior may reveal constraints rather than preferences. Multicultural people can also shift interpretive frames with context (Hong et al., 2000), so an earlier encounter may not supply the right script for this one.

Respect for cultural meaning does not require accepting discrimination, coercion, violence, exclusion, or an unsafe hierarchy as “just cultural.” Teams still need explicit standards for safety, truthfulness, consent, non-discrimination, and accountability. Explain their purpose and provide fair ways to challenge their implementation, rather than treating a powerful institution’s preferred standard as culturally neutral.

Cross-cultural experience can broaden cognition when people engage and adapt rather than merely travel; living abroad has been associated with creativity under such conditions (Maddux & Galinsky, 2009). If differences remain silent or unsafe, the information never reaches the decision.

**Step 5: Change the architecture.** Distribute the proposal in advance. Ask everyone to record risks independently. Invite the most junior or relevant expert before senior commentary. Use “What concern would we regret not discussing?” rather than “Does everyone agree?” Provide a private escalation path.

Once the same action can mean different things across audiences and relationships, influence cannot begin with the message alone. It must begin with the model through which the audience interprets it. Part V takes up that deliberate task through persuasion, communication, and repair.

The leaders are answering *Will this improve coordination?* Their audience is also asking *Will this cost me autonomy, and will the promised support arrive?* A correct answer to the first question cannot settle the others. To make progress, the proposal itself may need to change.

A useful starting point is therefore to identify what the audience expects and what evidence could change that expectation. Predictive processing offers a **theoretical analogy**, especially from perception and action: incoming information is compared with predictions, and discrepancies can lead to revision (Clark, 2013). The sequence in @tbl-25-model-update turns that idea into practical questions for a message; it is a design aid rather than a validated model of every persuasion process:

@tbl-25-barriers separates objections that another statistic can address from concerns requiring a change in governance, training, or workload. Listening may reveal a defect in the proposal rather than in its presentation.

Choose a product, policy, behavior-change request, difficult conversation, or research claim. In six lines, write: audience; desired response; current model; main barrier; credible evidence; constraint. Then write one observation that would genuinely discriminate the old model from your proposed one. If you cannot state that test, you may have a preference rather than a persuasive explanation.

Source credibility depends especially on perceived expertise and trustworthiness, although goodwill, similarity, status, confidence, and intent can also affect reception (Hovland & Weiss, 1951; Pornpitakpan, 2004). Credentials do not settle trust. A technically expert manager may still be an unsuitable messenger when earlier promises were broken or when the proposal benefits management at employees' expense. A different, conditional pattern is the **sleeper effect**: a message initially discounted because of a credibility warning can become more persuasive later. Kumkale and Albarracín’s (2004) meta-analysis found this delayed effect under particular message and discounting-cue conditions; it does not mean that every dubious claim grows persuasive with time.

For the platform proposal, a respected project leader who tested the system may be a more credible messenger than the chief technology officer alone. Yet a better messenger cannot substitute for verifiable governance. Employees need to know which data are recorded, who can see them, how the data may be used, and what recourse exists if the commitment is violated.

Evidence must answer the audience's actual question and match the claim being made. A demonstration can show that a workflow is possible; comparison data can estimate an effect; a case can illustrate a mechanism. Two-sided refutational messages can be especially useful for informed or skeptical audiences because they acknowledge consequential objections and answer them rather than pretending they do not exist (Hovland et al., 1949; O'Keefe, 1999). The test is not whether an objection was mentioned, but whether a reasonable skeptic can inspect the comparison, assumptions, uncertainty, and conditions under which the proposal would be withdrawn.

Emotion gives those consequences value. Different emotions orient attention and action differently, so “make it emotional” is not a scientific prescription (Lerner et al., 2015). Fear appeals are most defensible when the threat is real and the recommended response is both effective and feasible; fear without efficacy can produce avoidance or defensive control rather than protective action (Rogers, 1975, 1983; Witte, 1992). Hope, pride, compassion, anger, or humor may also affect motivation, but the relevant question is whether the feeling is proportionate to the evidence and points toward a feasible action.

For the platform, that means showing where duplication occurs, how the proposed workflow is expected to reduce it, what comparison produced the estimate, and which costs were included. The message can make avoidable frustration and pride in competent work salient. It should not manufacture fear of dismissal unless employment risk is real and openly addressed.

What encourages this thought? Motivation rises when the issue is relevant to a person’s goals; ability depends on knowledge, clear presentation, available time, and freedom from distraction. When both are high, argument quality generally matters more. When either is low, simple cues tend to carry more weight. More thought still does not guarantee a fair assessment: people can devote considerable effort to defending an identity or their initial position.

Petty, Cacioppo, and Goldman (1981) demonstrated this with a study about comprehensive exams. When the issue was highly relevant to students, strong arguments produced more persuasion than weak arguments. When relevance was low, source expertise mattered more. More generally, the same variable can play different roles: source expertise can operate as a simple cue, be treated as evidence relevant to the merits, change the motivation to think, bias the thoughts generated, or change confidence in those thoughts. Its role must be identified rather than inferred from the label *central* or *peripheral*.

The heuristic-systematic model, developed by Chaiken, makes a related distinction between systematic processing and heuristic processing (Chaiken, 1980; Chaiken et al., 1989). Systematic processing involves comparatively careful evaluation of message content. Heuristic processing relies on simple rules such as “experts can be trusted,” “longer messages are stronger,” “consensus implies correctness,” or “likable people are credible.” The processes can co-occur rather than forcing an either–or classification.

The **foot-in-the-door technique** starts with a small request before a larger related one. Freedman and Fraser (1966) found that agreement to an initial request could increase later compliance. The **door-in-the-face technique** begins with a larger request that is rejected, followed by a smaller one; Cialdini and colleagues (1975) studied how this apparent concession can encourage reciprocal compliance. Neither sequence guarantees success, and accepting a request does not establish that someone now believes the proposal is good. [Chapter 36](36-preparing-and-claiming-value.qmd#chapter-36-start) applies the distinction between concessions and independent value to bargaining.
A useful invitation leaves room to reject the pilot or change one's mind. A small initial “yes” should not hide later costs, manufacture obligation, or be treated as consent to a larger commitment.

The five-part route in @fig-story-update turns this change of explanation into a writing template. Ask what the protagonist believed, what challenged that belief, and what further evidence would justify changing it. Sara’s discovery of a previously unreported risk gives her a reason to investigate the meeting process; it does not yet establish which part of that process caused the silence.

Background earns attention when it helps resolve such a question. “Our organization was founded in 1986 and has always valued innovation” gives a reader little to investigate. “The new system solved the problem in every demonstration, yet no one used it” presents a discrepancy worth explaining. The opening needs enough context to make the difficulty intelligible, rather than a long history before the difficulty appears.

From outside the meeting, it is easy to tell Sara to stop supplying every answer. From her position, holding back means changing the very behavior she has regarded as helpful leadership. Readers need access to that tension to understand what the proposed change asks of her. **Identification** occurs when audience members imaginatively take the perspective of a character, share goals or emotions, and experience events partly from inside the character's situation. Identification differs from liking. You may identify with a character you do not entirely like because you understand their motives or feel their struggle from within.

Following a character can shift the question from “What do I think of this person?” toward “What would this situation be like from their position?” Sara need not be wholly admirable for readers to understand her wish to appear competent.

Small, Loewenstein, and Slovic (2007, Study 3) tested these three appeals with 159 people recruited on a university campus. Average donations were \$2.38 for the identifiable child alone, \$1.14 for statistics alone, and \$1.43 for the combined appeal. Adding the statistics reduced giving relative to the child alone. The result makes the design problem harder: information about scale can weaken the response that a personal account first creates. The study measured immediate donations from a small payment; it did not establish that withholding statistics leads to better-informed or more effective assistance.

A story can make an unfamiliar problem worth attending to, but its vividness cannot tell us how common the problem is. When you retell a case, carry that distinction with it: explain what the story illustrates and which broader claim still needs evidence.
[^ch31-shared-processing]: The neural measures concern coordinated processing under shared stimulation; they do not establish shared interpretations or beliefs.

A restaurant owner receives a pitch for a forecasting assistant. The first slide lists algorithms; the second celebrates the development team. By the third, the owner still cannot tell whether the tool will help decide how much food to prepare tomorrow.

Find out what makes trying the tool unattractive. The owner may doubt its accuracy, lack clean records, or worry that staff will treat recommendations as orders. Identity can also make a popular choice unattractive: Berger and Heath (2007) found more divergence from others in product domains that participants regarded as identity-signaling. For this owner, adoption might imply surrendering a valued skill. Ask whether that concern is present before treating it as the explanation. Once the concern is clear, choose a response that addresses it. A demonstration can address usability; a pilot may test forecasts; explicit override rules address control. If the product cannot meet an important constraint, the proposal needs work before the message does.

If a story would help, follow a person facing the decision. Picture the owner checking yesterday’s waste against today’s bookings, knowing that a cautious preparation plan could leave popular dishes unavailable. This scene gives the audience a goal and a trade-off. It does not need an invented crisis or a heroic founder.

The obstacle should make the proposed response worth considering. Perhaps the owner has sales records but cannot readily combine them into a daily forecast. That problem suggests a role for the tool. If the real problem is unreliable deliveries, better demand forecasts may help little.

Do not assume the audience’s current belief is a “misbelief” simply because it conflicts with the proposal. The pitch should reveal a limitation that can be investigated, with room for the investigation to vindicate the current practice.

In a fictional story, label the episode as imagined. In a factual case, report what was actually observed and what alternatives remain. An illustrative ending cannot establish demand, effectiveness, or savings; those claims need their own evidence.

For a brief version, try **AND–BUT–THEREFORE (ABT)**: the shared situation, the consequential difficulty, and the proposed response. Use it as a compression test. A **narrative index** based on counts of connecting words can flag a draft that keeps adding information without establishing a difficulty or consequence. Such a writing heuristic does not measure whether the causal argument is valid or whether an audience understands it. Inspect what the connections actually mean.
The ending requests a test proportionate to the evidence. It does not turn a promising demonstration into an established business result.

The owner needs to know whether using the software improves preparation enough to justify its cost. A demonstration that the software runs leaves that question open, just as observed adoption would not by itself show that users benefit. Even an established benefit may cost more to deliver than it is worth. Start by identifying the claim on which the decision depends, then use @tbl-27-claim-evidence to ask what evidence could test it and what that evidence would leave unestablished.

Not every message needs all six claim types. A policy recommendation may hinge on need, causal impact, distribution, and cost; an early prototype may appropriately make only a feasibility claim. For the **Reasons** row of STORY, record the pivotal claim, its type, the strongest available evidence, the relevant source or comparison, and what remains unestablished. If the available evidence cannot support the necessary claim, weaken the claim, change the requested action, or collect better evidence.

A clear layout and familiar language help the owner inspect the evidence. They can also make a weak claim feel comfortable: repetition increases familiarity, which can increase perceived truth (Hasher et al., 1977; Fazio et al., 2015). The distinction from [Chapter 13](13-accessibility-familiarity-and-ease.qmd#chapter-13-start) therefore matters when editing: make the comparison easier to check, rather than merely making the conclusion easier to repeat.

For the restaurant owner, show waste in units they can reconstruct—portions or ingredient costs over a stated period—and identify the comparison. Resolve the question that earned attention rather than using suspense to delay an inconvenient limitation.

A message built for the restaurant owner cannot simply be relabeled for a student, patient, or negotiating partner. Each faces a different decision and needs different evidence before acting; carrying over the scene while losing that decision turns adaptation into decoration. STORY travels across teaching, leadership, health, policy, entrepreneurship, and negotiation by preserving the questions that organize the message: start from the stakeholder's consequential decision, make the trouble specific, state the proposed mechanism, match reasons to claims, and end with an action that can be refused.

In teaching, a case should create the need for a concept and then yield to analysis. In leadership, a change story should acknowledge loss and protect valued identity rather than invent a “burning platform.” In health and policy, a patient or citizen story should be paired with prevalence, effects, alternatives, and uncertainty. In entrepreneurship, the stakeholder—not the product or founder—is usually the protagonist. In negotiation, a short story can explain why an interest matters without pretending that one side's account is the whole situation.
- **Evidence dump:** presenting impressive numbers that do not test the pivotal claim. State what each item of evidence should change and what it cannot establish.

Fictional story version: Maria had hired dozens of people and believed she was good at reading candidates. In one interview, a candidate from a familiar university spoke confidently about teamwork and leadership. Maria felt an immediate connection. Another candidate was quieter, less polished, and from an institution Maria did not know well. The team hired the first candidate. Six months later, performance problems appeared: missed deadlines, poor collaboration, and resistance to feedback. During a later review, Maria reread the interview notes and realized there were almost none. She had recorded impressions, not evidence. When the company introduced structured interviews, she resisted at first. They felt mechanical. But after using the same job-relevant questions and scoring evidence separately, she noticed something uncomfortable: her "intuition" had often been confidence responding to confidence. The structure did not replace her judgment. It gave her judgment something better to work with.

This story begins inside the manager's existing belief: "I can read people." It introduces a problem: a confident choice is followed by poor performance. It creates a turning point: rereading the notes reveals the absence of evidence. It offers a new model: structure improves judgment rather than replacing it. The example makes the reason for structure understandable; Chapter 41 examines the comparative evidence on structured judgment. Maria’s poor hiring outcome alone would not establish a flawed process. The missing job-relevant records are the reason she cannot evaluate that process reliably afterward.
This story explains an interest without revealing a reservation value. It humanizes the constraint and opens problem-solving rather than simply asserting a position.

A message worth sharing is not necessarily worth believing. People may pass content on because it expresses identity, creates connection, signals competence, helps someone, or supports collective action (Berger & Milkman, 2012; Falk et al., 2013; Baek et al., 2017). Optimize first for accuracy and inspectability, then for transmission.

An anecdote may illustrate a concept, and a case may contain a story. Use @tbl-27-1 to choose the form by the communication task; the labels describe overlapping uses rather than exclusive categories.

Build a **one-page STORY brief** for one research claim, policy, product, leadership request, or negotiation proposal. The single brief contains five rows: Shared reality, Trouble, Opportunity, Reasons, and Yes. In the Reasons row, identify the pivotal claim, classify it using @tbl-27-claim-evidence, give the strongest available evidence and comparison, state the uncertainty, and name what the evidence does not establish. At the bottom, answer three audit questions: Is any case presented as representative without a denominator? Can the audience meaningfully decline or revise the requested action? Which one sentence should be weakened or removed if the evidence is insufficient? Use the completed brief to deliver a 90-second message. Peer feedback identifies one unsupported inferential jump and one concrete repair. Working alone, mark every claim that needs outside evidence, check the pivotal one against its source, and revise the brief before delivering it again.

The manager and employees need to establish what problem they are meeting to solve. The feeling that they understand or attach similar meaning to the same event is one example of **shared reality** (Echterhoff et al., 2009). That perceived commonality does not require agreement on every issue, and it does not establish truth. Both sides could agree that someone ignored a deadline when the records show that the new date never reached them. Communication must make interpretations clear enough to examine, while evidence tests whether those interpretations fit what happened.

A useful design goal is **recoverability**: give the listener enough information to reconstruct the intended meaning and a way to correct an error. For example, a terse “Fine. Let’s discuss this tomorrow” leaves its tone and purpose uncertain. A fuller message explains the delay and invites a response: “I am too tired to give this a fair hearing tonight. I am not dismissing the concern. Could we discuss it at 09:00 tomorrow? If I have misunderstood what is urgent, tell me now.” The message cannot eliminate ambiguity, but it gives the other person a path to repair it.

Grice’s cooperative principle also helps explain communication. Grice (1975) argued that conversation is guided by expectations that speakers provide information that is relevant, truthful, sufficiently informative, and clear. Much meaning comes from these expectations. If someone says, “Some of the students passed,” listeners may infer that not all passed, even though the sentence does not logically say that. If someone asks, “Can you pass the salt?” the literal answer may be “yes,” but the intended meaning is a request.

Such **pragmatic inference** goes beyond the literal sentence to infer what a speaker means in context. People often say less than they mean because they expect listeners to make that inference. This makes communication efficient, but also fragile. Misunderstanding happens when people do not share the same assumptions.

This is especially clear in email and text communication. Kruger and colleagues (2005) found that people overestimate how well they can communicate tone over email. In Study 2, participants sent statements intended to be either sarcastic or serious. For email, senders expected about 78% correct interpretation and receivers judged themselves about 89% accurate, while actual accuracy was about 56%—not statistically distinguishable from the 50% chance benchmark. Voice raised accuracy to about 73%, although errors remained. These are results for a constrained tone-decoding task, rather than a general error rate for everyday email. The striking result is the gap: both sides can feel confident while reconstructing different tones. The sender thinks, “How could they not understand?” The receiver thinks, “How could they write such a thing?”

A curt reply seems to tell us how a colleague feels: “She is angry with me.” Responding to that anger may seem sensible, yet the reply could reflect an urgent task we cannot see. Defending ourselves before checking can introduce a dispute where there was only a hurried message. Inferring another person’s beliefs or intentions is often called **mentalizing** or **theory of mind**. We need it to cooperate and coordinate; the task is to keep the interpretation open to correction before acting on it.

One major error is egocentric projection: anchoring on one’s own perspective and insufficiently adjusting to another person’s perspective (Epley et al., 2004). We assume that our model of the world is closer to theirs than it really is. “I would not be offended by this feedback, so she should not be offended.” “I understood the email, so they should understand it.” “I enjoy this kind of small talk, so they must too.” “I would want direct advice, so they must want it.”

A related error is the false consensus effect: people overestimate how common their own beliefs, preferences, choices, and behaviors are (Ross et al., 1977). If I think an action is ethical, I may assume most reasonable people agree. If I dislike a policy, I may assume most people secretly dislike it too. If I would accept a risk, I may assume others would. Here the estimate concerns how widely a view is shared, rather than what one colleague thinks.

The same problem appears when we assume that readers recovered context we never stated. Looking for certainty in a face or gesture does not solve it: faces, bodies, and brief behavioral samples can contain information without becoming reliable dictionaries of a person's exact emotion, motive, or truthfulness (Ambady & Rosenthal, 1993; Barrett et al., 2019; DePaulo et al., 2003). Verbal information and direct questions are often more diagnostic than confident interpretation of isolated expressions (Gesn & Ickes, 1999; Hall & Schmid Mast, 2007). If something is important, do not rely on hints, microexpressions, or silence. State it, ask, and verify.

Across 25 experiments, Eyal, Steffel, and Epley (2018) found no overall accuracy improvement from instructions to take another person’s perspective. In their final experiment, direct conversation improved accuracy where imagining the other person’s perspective did not. Asking supplies information that imagination alone cannot, although its usefulness still depends on what the person knows and is willing to disclose.

For the manager, a useful question is: “When did you learn that the deadline had changed?” That may uncover a missing message rather than reluctance to accept responsibility. Follow with a paraphrase the colleague can correct: “So you were still working toward Friday because the new date was only discussed with the client team?”

At the meeting, each person first maps where they believed ownership changed. The manager asks for examples rather than motives. Participants reflect what they heard before defending a view. Differences become visible: one handoff was never defined, one deadline changed without reaching operations, and one employee interpreted an ambiguous sentence through a previous experience of blame. Those differences explain why the same instruction produced different responses. With the missing deadline message and unclear handoff identified, the group can assign the next action while keeping unresolved questions visible.

The same sentence in @fig-conversation-needs-map permits all three readings, so ask what kind of help is useful now rather than choosing a response from the words alone. A conversation may move between layers as the answer changes.

The manager cannot identify the colleague’s immediate need by deciding privately which conversation to have. A question gives the colleague a voice in that decision. Research on ordinary conversations suggests another benefit: Huang and colleagues (2017) found that people who ask more questions, especially follow-up questions, are better liked by their partners. Building on an answer can show that it received attention.

Depth does not mean forcing intimacy. It means allowing the conversation to move beyond labels into experience, meaning, emotion, values, needs, or identity when appropriate. Follow the last answer rather than reciting a prepared list. Ask for specificity, label emotion tentatively, invite correction, and move only one level deeper at a time.

Closeness depends on more than question depth. In a structured experiment, gradually escalating **reciprocal** self-disclosure produced greater immediate feelings of closeness between strangers than comparable small-talk tasks (Aron et al., 1997). In ongoing relationships, disclosure was more closely connected to intimacy when the partner was experienced as understanding, validating, and caring (Laurenceau et al., 1998). The lesson is not to reveal as much as possible. It is to disclose at an appropriate pace, notice whether the other person reciprocates voluntarily, and respond to what was entrusted rather than treating vulnerability as a technique.
When contact is safe and welcome, do not let an untested pessimistic forecast make the decision by itself. Leave the other person an easy way to decline.

Follow a point the other person has made rather than searching for the next question on a list. If the colleague says, “I felt you had already decided I was unreliable,” ask what in the message conveyed that verdict.
Choose the prompts that expose an uncertainty in your account, rather than asking the colleague to work through every category.

Validation shows that a partner’s meaning was noticed, understood, and incorporated. It may be as small as a precise “That makes sense because…” or “I see why that mattered.” It does not require endorsing every conclusion or action. Repeated, diagnostic signals—paraphrase, follow-up, acknowledgment, and specific appreciation—help build shared reality (Laurenceau et al., 1998; Rossignac-Milon et al., 2021).

A specific observation can still contain an inference. “You interrupted Anna twice” is easier to verify than “You made her feel unimportant.” If the impact on Anna matters, ask her rather than presenting your interpretation as her experience.

Warm honesty differs from nice silence, protective distortion, and “brutal honesty.” It combines care with information the other person can examine. Conflict is an interpersonal cycle: private intent becomes observable behavior, that behavior has an impact, and the response becomes observable behavior in the next turn. Good intent does not erase impact, and impact does not prove intent. Stay on your own side of the net: describe the observable behavior, own its impact on you or the work, name the relevant need, and make a testable request. Then ask across the net about the other person’s intent, constraints, and experience instead of declaring them.

A useful practice metaphor is **pinch → story → avoidance → crunch**; it names one possible escalation pattern, rather than a fixed sequence every conflict follows. A small disappointment creates a private story about motive. Avoidance prevents correction. The accumulating pattern later erupts as a large conflict. Raise the pinch while it is still observable: “When the agenda changed without notice, I felt unprepared. What happened?” In unsafe settings or strong power asymmetries, direct conversation may not be prudent; documentation, a representative, or formal support may be necessary.

Had the manager used this approach before sending the accusation, the opening could have been: “The section arrived after the client deadline, and I felt exposed because I had promised delivery. I may be missing information—when did you hear about the revised date?” Once the missing message became clear, both could discuss how deadline changes should be recorded and acknowledged. Inquiry belongs before the judgment about reliability; a request for earlier warning cannot repair a date the colleague was never given.

Moral reframing is also useful. A review by Feinberg and Willer (2019) describes evidence that political arguments can be more persuasive when framed in terms of the audience’s moral values rather than only the speaker’s. If someone values loyalty, authority, liberty, care, fairness, or purity differently than you do, repeating only your own moral language may fail. Translation is not manipulation when it remains truthful; it is respect for the listener’s moral world.
Then examine the evidence together and state what remains in disagreement. Respect makes the discussion possible; it does not require equal weight for claims with unequal support.

The colleague may still want time, an explanation, or a stronger safeguard. Forgiveness and reconciliation are separate decisions; an apology does not entitle the speaker to either. What can be checked is the promised correction and whether the next deadline change reaches the people responsible for it.

Suppose a builder expects early completion while a buyer fears delay. A fixed payment asks them to settle the price of that uncertain performance now, when their forecasts differ. The main questions concern measurement and control. Define completion so that speed cannot be achieved by omitting quality checks.
